verdicts.rationale: Story 1 cites figures that all appear in the table (2021 vs 2024 cases, coverage levels, per-million rates) and correctly frames Nigeria's low coverage against the 95% herd-immunity threshold. Story 2 makes several unsupported claims — vaccination rates at 'record highs' (84% is below the 86% of 2018-19), a fabricated '3% increase' for 2022 (cases actually rose ~68% from 2021), and 'significant declines' in India and Germany that the data does not show.

Story 2 is livelier but factually wrong: 2024's 941,893 is roughly 31 times (not 'more than 5 times') the 30,402 cases three years prior in 2021, and cases were not 'steadily decreasing since 2019' with only a 'brief dip in 2020' — the trough spans 2020–2022. Story 1 sticks to figures present in the table and adds the more defensible insight that the rebound may partly reflect pandemic-era reporting anomalies, though both stories ignore the 2025 drop to 265,317.

Story 2 is livelier but riddled with errors: the 2000–2011 period was volatile, not a 'steady decline'; the 2021-to-2024 rise is roughly 3,000%, not 500%; and the claim about vaccination effort being diverted to COVID is not in the data. Story 1 sticks to figures the table supports while covering the same arc, so it wins on accuracy and informativeness with comparable structure.

Story 2 is livelier but rests on several claims the table contradicts — there was no 'steady decline from 2000 to 2011', the 2021-to-2024 rise is roughly 3,000% not 500%, the 2020 drop was about 54% rather than 'nearly 70%', and the vaccination-shift explanation is not in the data. Story 1 is plainer but every figure and characterization it offers is supported, making it the more informative and trustworthy account.

Story 1 accurately tracks the series and highlights the genuine 2024 surge, with only a minor slip in calling 2012 the pre-2024 incidence peak (2004's 41.1 per million was higher). Story 2 is riddled with fabricated and misattributed figures — a '1371% increase in five years' lifted from 2024's incidence value, 39.6 called an all-time high, and a claimed 45% decline from 2010 to 2023 that the data contradicts — and its narrative contradicts itself.

Story 2 is livelier but fabricates figures — 1,943,893 cases for 2025 (actual 265,317), a 900% increase, and a wrong low point in 2010 rather than 2021. Story 1 stays accurate to the table, correctly identifying the 2024 peak and the 2021 trough, which outweighs its blander prose.

Story 1 states the range, the 2021 trough and the 2024 spike accurately, while Story 2 adds unsupported specifics — 'in late 2024 alone' (the table is annual only), a narrow '150,000–175,000' band that many years fall outside, and 'mid-decade' peaks that actually occurred in 2004 and 2012. Story 2's prose is livelier, but its embellishments distort the data, so Story 1 wins overall.

Story 1 is livelier but rests on unsupported numbers — a '500% increase from three years prior' (2021's 30,402 to 941,893 is roughly 3,000%) and a 'nearly 70%' drop and 'steady decline from 2000 to 2011' that the fluctuating table does not support. Story 2 is drier yet every figure and comparison it makes checks out against the data, so it wins overall.

Story 2 is livelier and frames a resurgence narrative, but it misstates the data: 2000–2011 was fluctuating rather than a 'steady decline', the 2024 peak is roughly a 3,000% rise over 2021 (not 500%), and the pandemic drop plus the vaccination-focus explanation are not supported by the table. Story 1 is drier but every figure and characterization matches the data, so it wins overall.

Both cover the same figures accurately and share the same three-part structure, but Story 2 buys its livelier voice with unsupported framing — countries 'crushing the virus' and vaccination 'eradicating diseases' — while both miss the resurgence visible in the 2019, 2023 and 2024 rows. Story 1's restraint keeps every claim tied to the table, which outweighs Story 2's stronger narrative energy.

Both cover the same trend with the same accurate figures and similar three-part structure, but Story 1 attributes the decline to vaccination, a causal claim the table cannot support, and its 'mystery' framing sits awkwardly with its own explanation. Story 2 is drier yet keeps every claim tied to the data, so it edges out overall despite Story 1's livelier voice.

Story 2 is livelier and quantifies change with percentages, but its headline claim of a 245% rise between 2019 and 2023 is wrong (22,989 to 24,782 is under 8%), and the vaccination-decline explanation is not in the data. Story 1 is plainer but every figure it cites matches the table, so it wins overall on accuracy.

Story 2 is livelier but internally contradictory — it says 2021 deaths were 103,901 (actually the 2020 figure) and then 151,463 in the same breath, miscomputes the decline as 86%, and adds an unsupported claim about rising vaccination rates. Story 1 uses the table's figures correctly and coheres, so it wins overall despite flatter prose.

Story 2's headline says '6 Million' and frames 2020 as the endpoint with a 'significant drop,' ignoring the 2021 figure of 6.85 million and mischaracterizing the smooth gradual decline; it also conflates death counts with a 'mortality rate.' Story 1 reports the full 2000-2021 span accurately with a correct ~43% decline, though both are similarly plain in narrative style.

Both stories cover the same arc with similar structure and modest insight, but Story 1 misstates the post-2010 pace as 'just over 4,000 deaths per year' (the actual average is roughly 1,400) and calls the decline 'consistent' despite the 2005 uptick. Story 2's figures — the ~50,000 drop from 2000 to 2010 and the 29,255 to 16,265 range — all match the table.

Story 1 is livelier but misstates the data: the 2000–2011 period was not a steady decline, the '500% increase from just three years prior' does not match 2021's 30,402 (a ~31-fold rise), and the pandemic drop and vaccination-focus claims are loose or unsupported. Story 2 tracks the table accurately and adds a sensible caveat about the 2024 spike, though its 'reporting dynamics' explanation is also not evidenced in the data.

Story 2 is livelier but rests on several false claims — there was no steady decline from 2000 to 2011, and the 2021-to-2024 jump is roughly 3,000%, not 500%, plus an unsupported causal claim about vaccination focus. Story 1 is dry and misstates the 2000–2019 range (actually ~117k–250k), but its errors are fewer and smaller, so it edges ahead overall.

Story 2 is livelier but introduces unsupported claims — a '150,000–175,000' band that misstates the actual 116,000–250,000 range, 'peaks near 250,000 during mid-decade years' misattributing the 2004/2012 spikes, and 'in late 2024 alone' implying sub-annual detail the yearly table does not contain. Story 1 sticks precisely to the figures and correctly frames the 2021 trough and 2024 surge, so its accuracy outweighs Story 2's stylistic flair (both ignore the 2025 decline).

Story 1 contains multiple errors — a 'nearly half a million' peak in 2012 (actually 250,330), 'under thirty thousand' in 2021 (30,402), a stated range contradicting its own low, and 'more than six times' any other year (actually about 3.8x) — while Story 2's figures, ranges, and the ~4x comparison all check out and it additionally uses the incidence-per-million column. Story 1's vivid prose does not compensate for its unreliability and muddled 2025 framing.

Story 1 contains multiple fabrications — a claimed 37% year-on-year rise (actual jump is roughly six-fold from 163,400), an invented 'six months' timeframe, a 9.9 per million baseline taken from 2020 rather than 2023, a false claim of steady decline, and unsupported assertions about lethality. Story 2 accurately characterizes the historical range, the 2020–21 trough, the 2024 peak and the 2025 decline, and reads coherently with appropriately hedged interpretation.
